text:
A police officer is at the scene of a murder. No witnesses. No camera footage. No obvious suspects or motives. Just a bit of hair on the sleeve of the victim’s jacket. DNA from the cells of one strand is copied and compared against a database. No match comes back, and the case goes cold. 

Corsight AI, a facial recognition subsidiary of the Israeli AI company Cortica, purports to be devising a solution for that sort of situation by using DNA to create a model of a face that can then be run through a facial recognition system. It is a task that experts in the field regard as scientifically untenable. 

Corsight unveiled its “DNA to Face” product in a presentation by chief executive officer Robert Watts and executive vice president Ofer Ronen intended to court financiers at the Imperial Capital Investors Conference in New York City on December 15. It was part of the company’s overall product road map, which also included movement and voice recognition. The tool “constructs a physical profile by analyzing genetic material collected in a DNA sample,” according to a company slide deck viewed by surveillance research group IPVM and shared with MIT Technology Review. 

Corsight declined a request to answer questions about the presentation and its product road map. “We are not engaging with the press at the moment as the details of what we are doing are company confidential,” Watts wrote in an email. 

But marketing materials show that the company is focused on government and law enforcement applications for its technology. Its advisory board consists only of James Woolsey, a former director of the CIA, and Oliver Revell, a former assistant director of the FBI.

The science that would be needed to support such a system doesn’t yet exist, however, and experts say the product would exacerbate the ethical, privacy, and bias problems facial recognition technology already causes. More worryingly, it’s a signal of the industry’s ambitions for the future, where face detection becomes one facet of a broader effort to identify people by any available means—even inaccurate ones.

This story was jointly reported with Donald Maye of IPVM who reported that “prior to this presentation, IPVM was unaware of a company attempting to commercialize a face recognition product associated with a DNA sample.”

A checkered past

Corsight’s idea is not entirely new. Human Longevity, a “genomics-based, health intelligence” company founded by Silicon Valley celebrities Craig Venter and Peter Diamandis, claimed to have used DNA to predict faces in 2017. MIT Technology Review reported then that experts, however, were doubtful. A former employee of Human Longevity said the company can’t pick a person out of a crowd using a genome, and Yaniv Erlich, chief science officer of the genealogy platform MyHeritage, published a response laying out major flaws in the research. 

A small DNA informatics company, Parabon NanoLabs, provides law enforcement agencies with physical depictions of people derived from DNA samples through a product line called Snapshot, which includes genetic genealogy as well as 3D renderings of a face. (Parabon publishes some cases on its website with comparisons between photos of people the authorities are interested in finding and renderings the company has produced.) 

Parabon’s computer-generated composites also come with a set of phenotypic characteristics, like eye and skin color, that are given a confidence score. For example, a composite might say that there’s an 80% chance the person being sought has blue eyes. Forensic artists also amend the composites to create finalized face models that incorporate descriptions of nongenetic factors, like weight and age, whenever possible. 

Parabon’s website claims its software is helping solve an average of one case per week, and Ellen McRae Greytak, the company’s director of bioinformatics, says it has solved over 200 cases in the past seven years, though most are solved with genetic genealogy rather than composite analysis. Greytak says the company has come under criticism for not publishing its proprietary methods and data; she attributes that to a “business decision.” 

Parabon does not package face recognition AI with its phenotyping service, and it stipulates that its law enforcement clients should not use the images it generates from DNA samples as an input into face recognition systems. 

Parabon’s technology “doesn’t tell you the exact number of millimeters between the eyes or the ratio between the eyes, nose, and mouth,” Greytak says. Without that sort of precision, facial recognition algorithms cannot deliver accurate results—but deriving such precise measurements from DNA would require fundamentally new scientific discoveries, she says, and “the papers that have tried to do prediction at that level have not had a lot of success.” Greytak says Parabon only predicts the general shape of someone’s face (though the scientific feasibility of such prediction has also been questioned). 

Police have been known to run forensic sketches based on witness descriptions through facial recognition systems. A 2019 study from Georgetown Law’s Center on Privacy and Technology found that at least half a dozen police agencies in the US “permit, if not encourage” using forensic sketches, either hand drawn or computer generated, as input photos for face recognition systems. AI experts have warned that such a process likely leads to lower levels of accuracy. 

Corsight also has been criticized in the past for exaggerating the capabilities and accuracy of its face recognition system, which it calls the “most ethical facial recognition system for highly challenging conditions,” according to a slide deck presentation available online. In a technology demo for IPVM last November, Corsight CEO Watts said that Corsight’s face recognition system can “identify someone with a face mask—not just with a face mask, but with a ski mask.” IPVM reported that using Corsight’s AI on a masked face rendered a 65% confidence score, Corsight’s own measure of how likely it is that the face captured will be matched in its database, and noted that the mask is more accurately described as a balaclava or neck gaiter, as opposed to a ski mask with only mouth and eye cutouts. 

Broader issues with face recognition technology’s accuracy have been well–documented (including by MIT Technology Review). They are more pronounced when photographs are poorly lit or taken at extreme angles, and when the subjects have darker skin, are women, or are very old or very young. Privacy advocates and the public have also criticized facial recognition technology, particularly systems like Clearview AI that scrape social media as part of their matching engine. 

Law enforcement use of the technology is particularly fraught—Boston, Minneapolis, and San Francisco are among the many cities that have banned it. Amazon and Microsoft have stopped selling facial recognition products to police groups, and IBM has taken its face recognition software off the market. 

“Pseudoscience”

“The idea that you’re going to be able to create something with the level of granularity and fidelity that’s necessary to run a face match search—to me, that’s preposterous,” says Albert Fox Cahn, a civil rights lawyer and executive director of the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, who works extensively on issues related to face recognition systems. “That is pseudoscience.”

Dzemila Sero, a researcher in the Computational Imaging Group of Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica, the national research institute for mathematics and computer science in the Netherlands, says the science to support such a system is not yet sufficiently developed, at least not publicly. Sero says the catalog of genes required to produce accurate depictions of faces from DNA samples is currently incomplete, citing Human Longevity’s 2017 study.

In addition, factors like the environment and aging have substantial effects on faces that can’t be captured through DNA phenotyping, and research has shown that individual genes don’t affect the appearance of someone’s face as much as their gender and ancestry does.  “Premature attempts to implement this technique would likely undermine trust and support for genomic research and garner no societal benefit,” she told MIT Technology Review in an email.

Sero has studied the reverse concept of Corsight’s system—“face to DNA” rather than “DNA to face”—by matching a set of 3D photographs with a DNA sample. In a paper in Nature Communications, Sero and her team reported accuracy rates between 80% to 83%. Sero says her work should not be used by prosecutors as incriminating evidence, however, and that “these methods also raise undeniable risks of further racial disparities in criminal justice that warrant caution against premature application of the techniques until proper safeguards are in place.”

Law enforcement depends on DNA data sets, predominantly the free ancestry website GEDmatch, which was instrumental in the search for the notorious “Golden State Killer.”  But even DNA sampling, once considered the only form of scientifically rigorous forensic evidence by the US National Research Council, has recently come under criticism for problems with accuracy.  

Fox Cahn, who is currently suing the New York Police Department to obtain records related to bias in its use of facial recognition technology, says the impact of Corsight’s hypothetical system would be disastrous. “Gaming out the impact this is going to have, it augments every failure case for facial recognition,” says Fox Cahn. “It’s easy to imagine how this could be used in truly frightening and Orwellian ways.”

The future of face recognition tech

Despite such concerns, the market for face recognition technology is growing, and companies are jockeying for customers. Corsight is just one of many offering photo-matching services with flashy new features, regardless of whether they’ve been shown to work. 

Many of these new products look to integrate face recognition with another form of recognition. The Russia-based facial recognition company NtechLab, for example, offers systems that identify people based on their license plates as well as facial features, and founder Artem Kuharenko told MIT Technology Review last year that its algorithms try to “extract as much information from the video stream as possible.” In these systems, facial recognition becomes just one part of an apparatus that can identify people by a range of techniques, fusing personal information across connected databases into a sort of data panopticon.

Corsight’s DNA to face system appears to be the company’s foray into building a futuristic, comprehensive surveillance package it can offer to potential buyers. But even as the market for such technologies expands, Corsight and others are at increased risk of commercializing surveillance technologies plagued by bias and inaccuracy.

Correction: An earlier version of this story said that Parabon NanoLabs has “solved over 600 cases”. The company has worked on over 600 cases, solving over 200.

Catching Rockets, Changing Worlds: How Heavy-Lift Transport Bridges Civilian, Military, and Humanitarian Frontiers
While the political world argued about Elon Musk, his engineers caught a spacecraft returning from orbit with giant steel arms. On November 14, SpaceX brought Starship home after 22½ hours in space and after deploying 26 Starlink satellites.

That deserves more than a passing glance. We are watching the beginnings of a transport revolution, and the possibilities should excite anybody who believes human ingenuity still matters.

While they have successfully captured the booster on previous flights, it was lost on this one; its reentry burn was apparently 1 second too long, and it didn't have enough fuel to hover long enough for capture.

But SpaceX's reusable design targets more than 100 metric tonnes to Earth orbit. The prize is moving heavy freight repeatedly, rather than throwing away expensive machinery after every delivery. As Musk often muses: “Imagine throwing away your corporate jet after every flight.”

Albertans understand that difference. You cannot build an oilsands project by hauling everything in the back of a pickup. Space development faces the same problem: equipment gets squeezed, folded, and shaved down because every kilogram costs money. Heavy, reusable transport could let engineers build for usefulness and durability instead.

The military is certainly paying attention, and the implications go well beyond putting soldiers in a rocket. Start with the satellites that help forces communicate and detect missiles. The U.S. Space Development Agency is building satellite networks with many smaller spacecraft, so losing a few does not cripple the system. Starship could help put large batches into orbit and replenish losses. An opponent would face a network that can be quickly rebuilt, rather than a handful of irreplaceable targets.

Then consider what larger spacecraft could carry: bigger antennas, more electrical power and more fuel for changing position. A communications platform could serve forces operating far from ground infrastructure; a servicing spacecraft could carry tools and replacement equipment. The military advantage is staying useful longer and restoring capability faster. Launch capacity puts more choices on the table.

Now consider urgent supplies. Imagine an isolated Pacific base needing replacement communications equipment, batteries and medical supplies while its usual transport routes are disrupted. A future rocket-delivery service could offer another way in. The value would lie in getting a critical load there when it matters, not competing with a freighter carrying next month's groceries.

Serious work is behind that idea. The Air Force's Rocket Cargo research began exploring aircraft-sized loads delivered through space. Its newer work increasingly emphasises reentry cargo pods: smaller containers that could separate from a launch vehicle and descend to different destinations. Starship could become the heavy hauler carrying those deliveries, without needing to land the entire spacecraft beside the troops.

An October experiment aboard SpaceX's Starfall capsule tested cargo environments using batteries, a water desalinator, survival gear and emergency medical equipment. Picture those supplies reaching stranded personnel or a disaster-stricken island. Safe delivery, unloading and launch readiness are the practical problems this research must solve. The humanitarian and military applications overlap for a simple reason: both sometimes need the right equipment somewhere difficult, quickly.

The same lifting power could transform civilian space activity. Larger satellite batches, bigger telescopes, space-station sections and repair equipment become easier to contemplate. Starlink provides an immediate customer and a reason to keep flying. Frequent use turns an impressive machine into a useful transport business. It would also give universities and smaller companies more room to try ideas, rather than making every experiment justify an extraordinary freight bill before it ever leaves the ground.

Now extend that supply line to the Moon. A lasting base needs power equipment, habitats, vehicles, water systems, food and spare parts. Think a huge construction camp, except nobody can drive into town for a replacement pump. Repeated heavy deliveries would allow crews to build something they can maintain and expand.

NASA's lunar plan uses tanker Starships to fill an orbiting depot, which fuels the lunar lander. Propellant transfer, an uncrewed landing and crew-safety certification are the major steps ahead. NASA is aiming for a 2028 crewed landing, with SpaceX and Blue Origin competing on readiness. This is how exploration starts becoming infrastructure.

How does the competition compare? On published low-Earth-orbit ratings, Blue Origin's New Glenn carries 45 tonnes and Europe's Ariane 64 carries 21.6. NASA's initial SLS configuration exceeds 95 tonnes but discards its stages. Sadly for Canada, I just don’t see Mark Carney’s taxpayer-funded Telesat on the competitive horizon. But I'm sure his friend who runs it is doing well. But all of these are different vehicles with different missions; Starship's ambition combines exceptional lifting capacity with recovery of both stages. That is an enormous commercial advantage to pursue.

The economics are straightforward. Imagine buying a new transport truck after every trip. Reuse spreads that machinery bill over repeated deliveries. Falcon has already shown the benefit: the U.S. Space Force said contract changes permitting booster recovery and reuse would save $52.7 million across the affected GPS missions.

Musk's eventual Starship cost target is below US$10 million per launch, potentially a few million with frequent flights. Achieving it while moving much larger loads would open opportunities that today's costs simply rule out.

Engineers, workers, suppliers and public partnerships deserve their share of the applause. So does the man willing to back difficult ideas and keep going when rockets explode and critics sneer.

In my judgment, Musk has contributed more to humanity than all his political detractors combined. They can keep arguing about the man. I would rather applaud what he and his people are building and the doors they are opening for the rest of us.

text:
40 Amazon Leo internet satellites were lost when ULA's Vulcan rocket failed 10 minutes into flight 🚀

The Vulcan lifted off from Cape Canaveral at 12:40 p.m. EST on Sunday, Nov 15. About 50 minutes later ULA said the rocket "suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit." The problem came during the Centaur upper stage burn; the cause is not yet known (ULA, Spaceflight Now, SpaceNews). It is the first outright failure of a ULA rocket since the company was formed in 2006, on only the fifth Vulcan flight and its first in nine months (Spaceflight Now, The Verge).

Why it matters: This was the first of 38 Vulcan launches Amazon has bought for Leo, its satellite internet rival to SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon needs more than 3,300 satellites for the full constellation, and this flight would have taken its total launched to 436. Vulcan now faces a failure investigation before it flies again; NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman offered NASA's help. Amazon also has launches booked on Blue Origin's New Glenn, Europe's Ariane 6 and SpaceX's Falcon 9 (Spaceflight Now, Space).

Also today:
• Jensen Huang has discussed returning as Nvidia's CEO with confidants, the Financial Times reported on Sunday; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the board should "go outside the company" and answer questions on export compliance within 10 days. Nvidia reports results on Tuesday, with analysts expecting $109 billion in quarterly revenue (Reuters, FT, LSEG)

• Astronomers traced mysterious radio pulses to a dead star, a white dwarf spinning every 8 minutes as it orbits a Sun-like star more than 5,000 light-years away (ICRAR, Curtin University, ScienceDaily)

40 satellites. 10 minutes. ULA's first outright failure since 2006.

text:
AMAZON $AMZN — 40 LEO SATELLITES DESTROYED IN ROCKET FAILURE. BUT THE BIGGER RISK ISN'T THE SATELLITES. IT'S THE LAUNCH BOTTLENECK.
I've been following Amazon's satellite broadband ambitions alongside SpaceX's Starlink expansion, and Sunday's launch failure highlights an important difference between building a satellite constellation and deploying one successfully.
Reuters reports that a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan rocket failed approximately 10 minutes after liftoff from Cape Canaveral, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites.
This is a setback for Amazon's effort to build a global satellite broadband network capable of competing with Starlink.
WHAT HAPPENED
🔹 40 Amazon Leo satellites were destroyed.
🔹 The Vulcan rocket failed approximately 10 minutes after launch.
🔹 ULA is jointly owned by Boeing $BA and Lockheed Martin $LMT.
🔹 The cause of the failure remains under investigation.
🔹 Amazon had previously deployed 398 satellites across 14 launches.
1. AMAZON'S BIGGER CHALLENGE IS DEPLOYMENT ECONOMICS
Amazon Leo represents a significant long-term opportunity, but building satellites is only one part of the business.
Amazon needs reliable launch capacity, sufficient orbital coverage, ground infrastructure and paying customers to turn that investment into sustainable revenue.
A failed launch creates more than the direct cost of lost satellites.
It can also delay constellation deployment, disrupt launch schedules and increase the capital required to reach commercial scale.
The financial impact will depend on insurance coverage, replacement costs, contractual protections and how quickly Amazon can secure replacement launch capacity.
Those details haven't been established.
2. SPACEX'S COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE IS BECOMING CLEARER
This is where I think the comparison with SpaceX becomes particularly interesting.
SpaceX has spent years improving Falcon 9's launch cadence, booster recovery and operational reliability.
That experience gives Starlink an important advantage in deploying and replenishing its satellite constellation.
Starship could eventually extend that advantage further if SpaceX achieves rapid, economically sustainable reuse.
But Starship's long-term economics are still being demonstrated.
The important distinction isn't simply which company builds better satellites.
It's which company can deploy more useful orbital capacity, more reliably and at a lower cost.
For satellite broadband, launch infrastructure is a strategic advantage.
3. ULA FACES A DIFFERENT EXECUTION CHALLENGE
For ULA, this incident raises questions about Vulcan's reliability and the potential implications for its future launch schedule.
An investigation will need to establish the cause before responsibility can be assigned.
I wouldn't automatically attribute the failure to Boeing, Lockheed Martin or Blue Origin's BE-4 engines without evidence.
But reliability is central to the economics and competitiveness of any launch provider.
Customers need confidence that valuable payloads can reach orbit safely and on schedule.
4. DOES THIS CHANGE MY AMAZON INVESTMENT THESIS?
No. I remain strongly bullish on $AMZN.
My core investment thesis is still built around AWS, AI infrastructure, advertising, marketplace economics and improving retail profitability.
Amazon Leo offers an additional long-term growth opportunity, but I don't currently treat it as a proven earnings or free-cash-flow driver.
The satellite business requires substantial upfront investment, and its eventual returns will depend on deployment costs, customer adoption, pricing and network utilisation.
One failed launch doesn't invalidate the opportunity.
But repeated delays or rising deployment costs could weaken its future economics.
MY TAKE
This incident reinforces something I've been watching across the AI and infrastructure investment cycle.
Capital investment creates potential capacity.
Operational execution turns that capacity into revenue.
And sustainable cash generation determines whether shareholders ultimately benefit.
Amazon has the financial resources to pursue satellite broadband over the long term.
But SpaceX has already demonstrated the strategic value of reliable, frequent launches through Falcon 9 and Starlink.
For me, the next questions are whether ULA can identify and resolve the failure, how quickly Amazon resumes deployment and whether Leo can eventually generate attractive returns on the capital invested.
I'm still bullish on Amazon. But this setback is a reminder that building a satellite network isn't just a technology challenge. It's a capital allocation, execution and cash-flow challenge.
And in that competition, launch reliability matters enormously.

7j/ • (~10:48, ~72:03) Oltmann, citing Cotton, says Maricopa hid a second EMS server from 2020 Senate auditors and overwrote security logs from the election period.

Fact check: Checks out: the 2021 Senate audit did report overwritten logs and an unproduced second device. Partly: Maricopa says it was an unused backup the Senate never requested, and that logs rolled over routinely. A later special-master review of routers and logs found no deletion or tampering, but was narrow and did not settle the backup-server question. Readers can weigh the rest.

7k/ • (~74:33) Oltmann says Cotton found two foreign IP addresses on a Dominion ICX used in November 2020, one in Taipei and one at a cloud provider in Germany.

Fact check: Doesn't hold up as evidence about Maricopa. Those addresses appear in Cotton's 2021 affidavit about an Antrim County, Michigan, device, not Maricopa's, and he wrote he could not tell when the data was created. Readers can weigh that.

The 2026–27 NHL season is roughly a quarter complete, and these charts offer a fascinating look at which teams are separating themselves from the pack.

The charts track wins above or below the league-average points percentage benchmark of .556 — not traditional standings.

🔥 THE TEAMS ON THE RISE:

🔴 CAROLINA HURRICANES (@Canes)

The defending Stanley Cup champions are absolutely flying.

Carolina has one of the most impressive trajectories on the entire NHL chart, soaring to the top of the Metropolitan Division.

Apparently, winning the Stanley Cup wasn’t enough. They’re interested in doing the whole thing again.

🟢 MINNESOTA WILD (@mnwild)

Minnesota’s trajectory is among the strongest in the league.

The Wild have established themselves as a major force in the Central Division, with their line climbing well above the league-average benchmark.

Is Minnesota becoming a legitimate Stanley Cup favourite?

🟠 EDMONTON OILERS (@EdmontonOilers)

Edmonton’s Pacific Division trajectory is absolutely remarkable.

While several divisional rivals have struggled, the Oilers have continued climbing and separating themselves from much of the competition.

🔴 NEW JERSEY DEVILS (@NJDevils)

New Jersey has been another standout in the Metropolitan Division.

Their upward trend shows a team creating meaningful separation from several divisional competitors.

🔵 TAMPA BAY LIGHTNING (@TBLightning)

Tampa Bay remains among the Atlantic Division’s strongest performers.

The Atlantic is competitive near the top, but the Lightning are showing why they cannot be overlooked.

📉 NOW FOR THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART…

🍁 TORONTO MAPLE LEAFS (@MapleLeafs)

The Leafs’ Atlantic Division trajectory has been heading sharply downward.

There is plenty of hockey remaining, but that’s not exactly a graph you want hanging in the dressing room.

🔵 VANCOUVER CANUCKS (@Canucks)

And then there’s Vancouver.

The Canucks’ trend falls so far below the regular chart that the original graphic literally extends the line off the bottom.

The chart even includes an annotation about Vancouver being 18.5 wins behind.

Someone might want to check whether that line has reached the basement yet.

📉 Elsewhere, Philadelphia, Chicago and several other clubs are also dealing with worrying trends.

🏒 WHAT THESE GRAPHS REALLY SHOW:

A team’s place in the standings doesn’t always capture how far above or below the league’s average performance it has been.

These charts offer another perspective on which teams are outperforming the benchmark, which teams are losing ground and where the biggest gaps are developing.

And after only roughly a quarter of the season, some of those gaps are already enormous.

1️⃣ Which team has been the BIGGEST positive surprise?

2️⃣ Which team’s performance has been the BIGGEST disappointment?

3️⃣ Are Carolina, Minnesota and Edmonton legitimate Stanley Cup favourites?

4️⃣ Can Toronto and Vancouver turn their seasons around?

text:
🔥 FOUR AMOUAGE MASTERPIECES FOR THE COMING WINTER!

Winter is approaching, and ordinary perfumes deserve a holiday! These four magnificent creations from the House of Amouage represent power, mystery, sophistication and extraordinary craftsmanship. From thunderous incense to aristocratic iris, intoxicating tobacco and uncompromising oud, each delivers its own unforgettable personality. Four fragrances. Four statements. Pure olfactory royalty.

1. AMOUAGE INTERLUDE 53 MAN

Perfumer: Pierre Negrin
THE EMPEROR OF SMOKE & INCENSE

Interlude 53 is not merely a perfume; it is an explosion of confidence, mystery and commanding masculinity. Its magnificent concentration transforms smoky incense, dark resins and luxurious woods into an unforgettable experience. Deep, dramatic and uncompromising, this masterpiece belongs to gentlemen who appreciate extraordinary intensity and refuse to smell ordinary.

NOTES & PERFORMANCE — 

Oregano, pimento berry, bergamot, frankincense, opoponax, amber, leather, oud, patchouli and sandalwood create an extraordinary smoky composition. Exceptional longevity, often 12–16+ hours, with powerful projection and tremendous persistence. Best reserved for cold evenings and confident, controlled application.

2. AMOUAGE OPUS XIV ROYAL TOBACCO

Perfumer: Cécile Zarokian

THE KING OF TOBACCO & ORIENTAL OPULENCE
Royal Tobacco is a magnificent journey into aristocratic luxury. Imagine an exclusive gentlemen's lounge filled with aromatic tobacco, ancient incense, exotic spices and precious woods. Rich, mysterious and beautifully constructed, it possesses extraordinary depth without sacrificing refinement. Every passing hour reveals another luxurious dimension of this exceptional winter masterpiece.

NOTES & PERFORMANCE — 

Tobacco absolute, frankincense, cardamom, anise, fenugreek, vanilla, benzoin, myrrh, oud and woods create a rich, spicy, resinous composition. Longevity commonly reaches 10–14+ hours, with commanding initial projection and impressive sillage. Particularly magnificent during cold winter nights.

3. AMOUAGE OPUS XIII SILVER OUD

Perfumer: Cécile Zarokian

THE DARK LORD OF ANIMALIC OUD

Silver Oud is uncompromising perfumery for serious collectors. Dark, mysterious, animalic and intensely woody, it explores the raw beauty of oud without attempting to please everybody. Its leathery warmth, earthy darkness and extraordinary depth create a commanding presence. This is not casual fragrance territory; it demands appreciation, confidence and character.
NOTES & PERFORMANCE — 

Cypriol, patchouli, Virginia cedar, oud, castoreum, vanilla and ambrarome produce a dark, leathery, animalic woody signature. Frequently reported longevity exceeds 12 hours, with strong projection and remarkable clothing persistence. A challenging, powerful fragrance particularly suited to colder weather.

4. AMOUAGE INTERLUDE BLACK IRIS MAN

Perfumer: Pierre Negrin

THE ARISTOCRAT OF DARK ELEGANCE

Black Iris takes the legendary Interlude character into a more polished, sophisticated universe. Luxurious orris softens the smoky incense, while rich resins and precious woods create remarkable depth. It is mysterious without being aggressive, powerful without becoming overwhelming, and exceptionally elegant. A distinguished winter companion for refined gentlemen.

NOTES & PERFORMANCE — 
Bergamot, rosemary, violet leaves, orris, frankincense, myrrh, amber, labdanum, vanilla, leather, oud, sandalwood and patchouli create remarkable depth. Expect approximately 10–14 hours of longevity, strong initial projection and refined sillage. Particularly beautiful during elegant winter evenings and formal occasions.

♦ MY WINTER VERDICT

INTERLUDE 53 — For explosive smoky power.

ROYAL TOBACCO — For luxurious tobacco and spicy warmth.

SILVER OUD — For uncompromising animalic darkness.

BLACK IRIS — For extraordinary gentlemanly elegance.

FOUR MASTERPIECES. FOUR PERSONALITIES. ONE HOUSE — AMOUAGE!

I would happily reserve all four for the coming winter. Each offers a genuinely different experience, rather than four variations of the same fragrance.

Performance figures are approximate wear reports, not guaranteed results. Skin, temperature and application affect longevity and projection.

text:
Jumping between ten different tabs, connecting your wallet to separate platforms, and getting lost across fragmented interfaces is one of the most exhausting parts of navigating crypto. The desire to consolidate daily operations under a single roof is what makes the Web3 "super-app" concept consistently appealing.

Quad Cell, the second project featured at the November 11 Builder Hub event, is a prototype built to eliminate this fragmentation. Its goal is to bring prediction markets, perpetual futures, AI-assisted payments, and real estate discovery together on a single screen through one wallet connection.

Yet, how does packing four vastly different verticals into one interface work in practice? Let’s look at the conveniences the platform offers alongside the architectural questions it leaves unanswered.

Key Advantages of Quad Cell

❖ Multi-Vertical Experience in One Interface: Without switching protocols, users can take "Yes/No" positions across sports, politics, and tech, open perpetual positions with up to 50x leverage, and browse real estate listings in Dubai from a single dashboard. This setup promises a streamlined front-end experience that saves time and reduces tab fatigue.

❖ Chat-Based Transactions and Information Assistant: The built-in AI assistant serves two practical functions. On one hand, it pulls data from sources like CoinGecko to provide real-time updates on trending assets, DeFi TVL, and the Fear & Greed Index. On the other, it translates simple text prompts (such as specifying a recipient address and amount) directly into a prepared transaction ready for wallet approval.

❖ Non-Custodial Signing Flow: In the AI-assisted payment flow, the assistant only drafts the transaction rather than executing it autonomously. Leaving the final signature strictly within the user’s wallet is a sound security choice.

Current Shortcomings and Disadvantages

❖ Lack of Shared Infrastructure and Capital Efficiency: Although four distinct products sit on the same screen, they do not share a unified margin system, a common oracle layer, or account abstraction in the background. As the founder openly noted, the only common thread right now is the shared wallet connection and interface. This makes the platform function more like a front-end aggregator of separate tools rather than a deeply integrated financial protocol.

❖ Oracle and Resolution Ambiguity in Prediction Markets: For prediction markets running on a parimutuel pool model, the most critical element is how real-world outcomes are verified on-chain. While the presentation emphasized smart contract pool security, it left unanswered which oracle feeds determine the winning side and how disputes or incorrect outcomes are handled.

❖ Diluted Focus and Surface-Level Real Estate Integration: Perpetual futures trading and physical real estate transactions belong to entirely different worlds with vastly different legal requirements. Currently, the real estate module mainly consists of an AI summarizing property listings in Dubai, with no concrete demonstration of on-chain title transfers or legal documentation workflows prior to mainnet.

❖ Unclear Rialo Integration Scope: With demo transactions executed on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet, the technical scope of how Rialo’s architecture actively powers or connects these four modules was not explained during the session.

Overall Assessment

Quad Cell takes a bold and user-centric approach to solving one of Web3’s biggest hurdles: fragmented user experience. Its vision of consolidating diverse financial tools under a single wallet connection, paired with an intuitive AI assistant that prepares transactions from plain text prompts, genuinely simplifies day-to-day crypto interactions. Bringing four distinct verticals together into a functional interface at the prototype stage is a promising foundation. As the project matures, solidifying back-end details like oracle verification and weaving in Rialo’s native capabilities could position Quad Cell as a powerful, all-in-one hub that makes navigating Web3 effortless for everyday users.

text:
I owe an honest admission.

I was so focused on protecting General Jensen at all costs that I forgot about Jensen the man. Whether he comes back, works with Elon, or leads TSMC is his family's business, not mine. So let me stop and simply honor him and his family.

Something deeper may be going on. I'm not a psychologist, but I know when it's time for soul searching. This isn't about America or AI anymore. It's about Jensen and his family.

Jensen, take the time you need. If I'm honest, take the rest of your life for yourself and your family. The world will keep moving. As much as I'd love to see you return, I'd rather see you build a new life, heal, and enjoy the fruits of your labor. You love food, you love Taiwan, and there's so much more out there. Your family was there before the fame, before the shareholders, before the governments, before TSMC. They supported you then. Focus on them now.

I take back every statement I made. I was being selfish. Jensen the hero has earned his rest.

I speak as a combat veteran who walked away at the top of my game. I came close to dying many times serving my country, and later in the top-secret work I did for private companies. I loved that work. Even with an offer from SpaceX AI on the table, I chose life over service. I had to learn to love myself and my life more than the mission, and in that recovery I grew, adapted, and evolved. I'm reaching out with the same love and understanding I had to find for myself.

I'm semi-retired now and still create value here and there, but the above-and-beyond sacrifice now belongs to me and my family. A new chapter isn't the end. It's a shift: 80% family and self, 20% innovation and creation.

Jensen, you're free to never return. Life is short, and you've already served this country and your fellow humans with honor. There's zero shame in building the largest company in the world, lifting up your employees and their families, and then walking off into the sunset. You're still the GOAT, and I'll respect whatever you decide.

You can grow from this pain, but you don't owe us anything more. Your debt now is only to yourself and your family. Instead of demanding more sacrifice from you, it's time we repay you with gratitude.

There are two kinds of people: those who don't know how to create value, and those who don't know when to stop. We all say family comes first, yet we keep walking out the door and starving the people we love of our time. We say we have to provide, or that we love what we do. I get it. I love what I do too, but I love my family and myself more and let's be honest we all do.

The most important things in life deserve our best attention, love, and time. Your wife and family deserve that far more than America, the tech industry, or your employees ever will and I'm sure they will support it. You've served us well. Now let us give you peace and respect.

from a Sensitive Combat Retire Veteran 🤣 Semper Fi Jensen

As much as I'd love to see you return, I'd rather see you build a new life, heal, and enjoy the fruits of your labor. You love food, you love Taiwan, and there's so much more out there. Your family was there before the fame, before the shareholders, before the governments, before TSMC. They supported you then. Focus on them now.

I take back every statement I made. I was being selfish. Jensen the hero has earned his rest.

I speak as a combat veteran who walked away at the top of my game. I came close to dying many times serving my country, and later in the top-secret work I did for private companies. I loved that work. Even with an offer from SpaceX AI on the table, I chose life over service. I had to learn to love myself and my life more than the mission, and in that recovery I grew, adapted, and evolved. I'm reaching out with the same love and understanding I had to find for myself.

I'm semi-retired now and still create value here and there, but the above-and-beyond sacrifice now belongs to me and my family. A new chapter isn't the end. It's a shift: 80% family and self, 20% innovation and creation.

Jensen, you're free to never return. Life is short, and you've already served this country and your fellow humans with honor. There's zero shame in building the largest company in the world, lifting up your employees and their families, and then walking off into the sunset. You're still the GOAT, and I'll respect whatever you decide.

You can grow from this pain, but you don't owe us anything more. Your debt now is only to yourself and your family. Instead of demanding more sacrifice from you, it's time we repay you with gratitude.

There are two kinds of people: those who don't know how to create value, and those who don't know when to stop. We all say family comes first, yet we keep walking out the door and starving the people we love of our time. We say we have to provide, or that we love what we do. I get it. I love what I do too, but I love my family and myself more and let's be honest we all do. 

The most important things in life deserve our best attention, love, and time. Your wife and family deserve that far more than America, the tech industry, or your employees ever will and I'm sure they will support it. You've served us well. Now let us give you peace and respect.

from a Sensitive Combat Retire Veteran 🤣 Semper Fi Jensen

text:
🌊 100 Facts About the Dead Sea, the Lowest Place on Earth

🌍 GEOGRAPHY & RECORDS

𝟏. Its shore is the lowest land on Earth, roughly 430+ m (1,410+ ft) below sea level, and it keeps getting lower.

𝟐. Despite the name, it is not a sea but a landlocked salt lake with no outlet: water leaves only by evaporation.

𝟑. It borders Jordan 🇯🇴 to the east and Israel 🇮🇱 and the West Bank to the west.

𝟒. Its main source of water is the Jordan River, which flows in from the north.

𝟓. It lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, on a fault where the Arabian plate slides past the African (Sinai) plate 🧩.

𝟔. That sideways motion is only a few millimetres a year, but over millions of years it has opened a deep basin.

𝟕. The lake is now roughly 50 km (31 mi) long and up to about 15 km (9 mi) wide.

𝟖. It is about 300 m (nearly 1,000 ft) deep, making it one of the deepest hypersaline lakes in the world.

𝟗. The Lisan Peninsula, on the Jordanian side, splits the lake into a deep northern basin and a once-shallow southern basin.

𝟏𝟎. The southern basin dried up naturally as the level fell and is now mostly industrial evaporation ponds.

𝟏𝟏. In Hebrew it is Yam ha-Melah, the "Sea of Salt"; in Arabic, al-Bahr al-Mayyit, the "Dead Sea".

𝟏𝟐. Another Arabic name is Bahr Lut, the "Sea of Lot".

𝟏𝟑. Greek and Roman writers called it Lake Asphaltites, after the lumps of bitumen (asphalt) that floated on it.

𝟏𝟒. The region is a desert: the shores get only about 50–100 mm (2–4 in) of rain a year 🏜️.

𝟏𝟓. Summer temperatures routinely top 40 °C (104 °F).

𝟏𝟔. Because the shore is so low, air pressure there is about 5% higher than at sea level, so each breath holds slightly more oxygen.

𝟏𝟕. The thick air and haze filter UV light, which is said to make sunburn less likely than at the same latitude elsewhere ☀️.

𝟏𝟖. Mount Sodom, near the southern end, is a ridge about 11 km long made mostly of rock salt.

𝟏𝟗. Malham Cave inside Mount Sodom was mapped at about 10 km in 2019, making it one of the longest salt caves known.

𝟐𝟎. A salt pillar on Mount Sodom is popularly called "Lot's Wife", after the biblical story.

🧂 SALT, WATER & LIFE

𝟐𝟏. Its water is about 34% salt, nearly ten times saltier than the ocean (about 3.5%).

𝟐𝟐. It is not the saltiest lake on Earth: Lake Assal in Djibouti 🇩🇯, Don Juan Pond in Antarctica 🇦🇶 and Gaet'ale Pond in Ethiopia 🇪🇹 are saltier.

𝟐𝟑. The water is about 1.24 times as dense as fresh water, so people float almost without effort.

𝟐𝟒. Normal swimming is hard: your legs pop up and you bob like a cork.

𝟐𝟓. Unlike seawater, which is mostly sodium chloride, it is rich in magnesium and calcium chlorides.

𝟐𝟔. That mix makes the water feel oily and slippery on the skin.

𝟐𝟕. It is one of the world's richest natural sources of bromine.

𝟐𝟖. Getting the water in your eyes is extremely painful, and swallowing it can be dangerous ⚠️.

𝟐𝟗. Fish carried in by the Jordan River soon die in the salty water 🐟.

𝟑𝟎. It is not completely dead: salt-loving microbes live in it.

𝟑𝟏. In 1936, microbiologist Benjamin Elazari Volcani showed that microbes survive in its water.

𝟑𝟐. The microbe Haloferax volcanii, first isolated from Dead Sea mud, is now a standard lab organism.

𝟑𝟑. After very rainy winters in 1980 and 1992, blooms of algae and microbes tinted the surface red.

𝟑𝟒. Divers found freshwater springs on the lake floor, coated with mats of microbes, in a 2011 study 🤿.

𝟑𝟓. For centuries the lake was layered, but around 1979 it "turned over" and mixed from top to bottom.

𝟑𝟔. Salt now settles on the deep lake floor as a growing layer of halite crystals, reportedly about 10 cm a year.

𝟑𝟕. Evaporation removes more than a metre of water from its surface each year.

𝟑𝟖. Its shores are lined with white salt crusts, salt "mushrooms" and crystal-covered rocks.

𝟑𝟗. Lumps of bitumen used to float up from the lake bed, especially after earthquakes.

𝟒𝟎. Its black mineral mud is sold around the world for skin care 🧖.

📉 THE SHRINKING SEA

𝟒𝟏. The surface is falling by more than 1 m (3 ft) a year.

𝟒𝟐. In the early 20th century the surface was about 390 m below sea level; today it is roughly 438 m.

𝟒𝟑. Its surface area has shrunk by about a third since the 1960s.

𝟒𝟒. The main cause is upstream use of Jordan River water for farms and cities by the countries of the basin.

𝟒𝟓. The Jordan once delivered over a billion cubic metres of water a year; today only a small fraction arrives.

𝟒𝟔. Mineral companies' evaporation ponds also account for a significant share of the water loss.

𝟒𝟕. More than 6,000 sinkholes have opened along its shores since the 1980s 🕳️.

𝟒𝟖. They form when fresh groundwater dissolves buried salt layers left behind by the retreating lake.

𝟒𝟗. Sinkholes have swallowed roads, date palm groves and beach facilities, and some beaches have closed.

𝟓𝟎. In the south, salt building up in the industrial ponds raises their level, so salt is now being harvested to protect nearby hotels.

𝟓𝟏. At some beaches, signs mark where the shoreline was decades ago, now far from the water.

𝟓𝟐. A Red Sea–Dead Sea water pipeline was planned for years to refill the lake, but the project stalled.

𝟓𝟑. The idea of a canal to the Dead Sea dates back to the 1850s, when British writer William Allen proposed one.

𝟓𝟒. Cores drilled from the lake floor in 2010–2011 suggest it nearly dried up during a warm period about 120,000 years ago.

𝟓𝟓. During the last Ice Age, a much larger lake called Lake Lisan stretched from the Sea of Galilee to south of today's Dead Sea.

🏺 HISTORY & ARCHAEOLOGY

𝟓𝟔. Jericho, just north of the lake, is often called one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns, settled over 10,000 years ago.

𝟓𝟕. Ancient Egyptians used Dead Sea bitumen in mummification, according to chemical studies of mummies.

𝟓𝟖. Aristotle described a lake so bitter that no fish lived in it and people could not sink.

𝟓𝟗. Antiquity's famous balsam perfume was grown at the oasis of Ein Gedi on the western shore 🌿.

𝟔𝟎. A synagogue mosaic at Ein Gedi curses anyone who reveals "the secret of the town", thought to be the balsam recipe.

𝟔𝟏. Mark Antony is said to have given Cleopatra rights to the region's bitumen and balsam.

𝟔𝟐. King Herod built the fortress-palace of Masada on a mesa overlooking the lake.

𝟔𝟑. According to historian Josephus, 960 people died at Masada in 73/74 AD rather than surrender to Rome.

𝟔𝟒. The Roman siege ramp at Masada is still visible today; Masada became a UNESCO site in 2001.

𝟔𝟓. On the Jordanian side, Josephus places the execution of John the Baptist at the fortress of Machaerus.

𝟔𝟔. Al-Maghtas, the baptism site near the lake's northern end, was listed by UNESCO in 2015.

𝟔𝟕. The 6th-century Madaba Map mosaic in Jordan shows the Dead Sea with boats, and fish turning back from its salty water 🗺️.

𝟔𝟖. Bronze Age sites such as Bab edh-Dhra in Jordan are sometimes linked to the biblical Sodom and Gomorrah.

𝟔𝟗. A Byzantine monastery near Safi in Jordan was built around the cave traditionally linked to Lot.

𝟕𝟎. In 1961, more than 400 copper objects about 6,000 years old were found in a cave at Nahal Mishmar.

𝟕𝟏. A Chalcolithic temple at Ein Gedi is roughly 5,500 years old.

𝟕𝟐. Irish explorer Christopher Costigan sailed the lake in 1835 and died soon after the trip.

𝟕𝟑. In 1848, a US Navy expedition led by William Lynch mapped and measured the lake 🚣.

𝟕𝟒. An earthquake in 1927 centred near the Dead Sea killed about 500 people across the region.

𝟕𝟓. In 2021, a cave in the Nahal Hever canyon yielded a woven basket thought to be about 10,500 years old 🧺.

📜 THE DEAD SEA SCROLLS

𝟕𝟔. In 1946–47, according to the usual account, a Bedouin shepherd searching for a lost goat found ancient scrolls in a cave at Qumran.

𝟕𝟕. Over the next decade, about 900 manuscripts were recovered from 11 caves near Qumran.

𝟕𝟖. They date from roughly the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD.

𝟕𝟗. They include the oldest known manuscripts of books of the Hebrew Bible.

𝟖𝟎. The Great Isaiah Scroll is almost complete and about 7.3 m (24 ft) long.

𝟖𝟏. The Temple Scroll, at about 8 m, is the longest of them.

𝟖𝟐. Most are written in Hebrew, with others in Aramaic and Greek, mostly on parchment.

𝟖𝟑. The Copper Scroll lists hidden treasure that has never been found 💰.

𝟖𝟒. In 1954, four scrolls were offered for sale in a small Wall Street Journal advertisement.

𝟖𝟓. In 2021, new scroll fragments were found in the Cave of Horror, the first such find in about 60 years.

𝟖𝟔. Fragments bought by a US museum in the 2010s were later shown to be modern forgeries.

𝟖𝟕. The Copper Scroll is displayed at the Jordan Museum in Amman 🇯🇴.

🧖 HEALTH, NATURE & INDUSTRY

𝟖𝟖. Two large mineral companies operate here: Dead Sea Works 🇮🇱 and the Arab Potash Company 🇯🇴.

𝟖𝟗. They extract potash for fertiliser, plus bromine, magnesium and salt.

𝟗𝟎. Dead Sea Works grew out of the Palestine Potash Company, founded around 1930 by engineer Moshe Novomeysky.

𝟗𝟏. Clinics on its shores offer sun-and-sea "climatotherapy" for psoriasis, and studies report improvement for many patients.

𝟗𝟐. The classic tourist photo is someone floating on their back and reading a newspaper 📰.

𝟗𝟑. Highway 90 along the western shore is among the lowest roads in the world 🛣️.

𝟗𝟒. Wadi Mujib in Jordan, a canyon that drains into the lake, is billed as the lowest nature reserve on Earth.

𝟗𝟓. Ein Gedi is home to Nubian ibex and rock hyraxes 🐐.

𝟗𝟔. Hundreds of millions of migrating birds pass over the rift valley each spring and autumn 🦅.

𝟗𝟕. In 2011, the Dead Sea was one of the finalists in the New7Wonders of Nature vote.

𝟗𝟖. Artist Sigalit Landau sank a black dress in the lake; months later it came out covered in white salt crystals 👗.

𝟗𝟗. Floods from desert canyons can briefly turn the lake's edge muddy brown after rare winter storms ⛈️.

𝟏𝟎𝟎. Visitors are advised to stay in the water only about 10–20 minutes at a time and to rinse off afterwards 🚿.

text:
Who Are These Australians?

For sixty thousand years and more,
First Peoples knew this land:
its rivers, stars and seasons,
its ochre held in hand.

Then came the new chums over seas—
English, Scottish, Irish too,
with colonial bibs and bobs,
and flags the wind blew through.

Gold glittered; Chinese settlers came.
Indians and Afghans made lives here too,
their stories woven through this land
before the nation knew.

Then laws were raised to bar non-whites:
a plain-vanilla dream.
But lives already rooted here
ran deeper than that scheme.

Two world wars passed. The cry went up:
“Populate or perish.”
From Europe came the displaced,
including Jewish refugees,
with memories and children
and hopes they came to cherish.

Later, Turkish arrivals came
beneath a widening sky.
Then Vietnam burned, and refugees
found shores where they could try

to build again. Al Grassby spoke:
“Australia will be multicultural.”
And people married across old lines;
new families filled the schools.

The population changed; more doors
swung open than before.
Chinese and Indian newcomers came,
and brought their gifts ashore.

The GDP grew; living standards rose;
new flavours filled the street—
a thousand kitchens sending out
their welcome and their heat.

Then Pauline Hanson offered blame,
sold racism as a cure:
“Australia for Australians”—
as though that made us pure.

But who are these Australians?
Look round the table spread:
First Peoples, old and newer homes,
and all the roads that led

to children sharing stories,
to hands that pass the bread—
a land for all who call it home,
with room for more ahead.

text:
ONE in four teenagers from a Protestant background would like to learn Irish.

The survey of post-primary pupils, published by the Department for Communities, found 26% of respondents from a Protestant background said they would like to learn Irish, whether at school, online, from family and friends or at community classes. 
School was the most popular option, with 16% of Prot-would like to learn Irish in the classroom. Interest in the language far outstrips current knowledge, with just 8% of Protestant pupils saying they have any Irish. 
Strong interest in Irish language from Protestant young people ‘no surprise’ says Turas spokesman
Niall Páirc, deputy manager of the east Belfast Irish language project Turas, said the findings came as no surprise, as many of its learners are Protestant. 
“We’ve seen how attractive the Irish language has become over the past number of years, and a lot of our learners are Protestants,” he said. 
“So no, it wouldn’t surprise us to see that.” 
He said there was “a general exploration of language and identity these days, which maybe people weren’t thinking about in past decades, especially during the conflict”. 
Mr Páirc said many state schools did not offer Irish, often because of staffing pressures and a lack of demand. 
“We do a lot of school outreach, and we’ve noticed that in a lot of the state schools there just isn’t Irish language available,” he said. 
“That’s down to a whole host of reasons. Staffing is a big issue, and if there’s not enough interest, schools can’t really justify the money for an Irish department. 
“Our dream would be for more schools in the area to have a dedicated Irish department in the future, if there was enough growth, enough interest and enough support.” 
The Young Persons’ Behaviour and Attitudes Survey, carried out by the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency, questioned pupils in Years 8 to 12 at 90 post-primary schools between September 2025 and February 2026. 
Just over half of Catholic pupils (51%) have some knowledge of Irish, meaning they can understand, speak, read or write it, compared with 8% of Protestant pupils and 11% of those of other or no religion. 
Some 37% of Catholic pupils said they could speak Irish, compared with 3% of Protestant pupils. Overall, 30% of pupils have some Irish. However, the language is not universally popular among Catholic pupils, almost three in 10 of whom said they did not want to learn it. 
Mr Páirc said that reflected a wider problem with languages. 
“I just think the vast majority of people aren’t really interested in languages,” he said. 
“It’s hard to get people interested in any language, including Irish. You see that in the number of pupils taking languages at GCSE and A-level. Languages and the arts in general have been really struggling.” 
He added that attempts to link Irish with politics did not help. 
“The Irish language has its own discourse around it that we see every day in the media, and that certainly doesn’t help, whether it’s an attempt to link it with politics and division,” he said. 
Knowledge of Irish was highest among the youngest pupils, at 40% of those in Year 8 compared with 20% in Year 12. Those who do have Irish tend to use it, with a quarter saying they speak it every day and a further third weekly. 
One in five of them said they could hold a complicated conversation in the language. The survey found almost exactly the same level of interest in Ulster-Scots, with 27% of Protestant pupils and a quarter of Catholic pupils saying they would like to learn it. 
Overall, 10% of pupils have some knowledge of Ulster-Scots, rising to 16% among Protestant pupils, while just 3% said they could speak it. 
A Department for Communities spokesperson said, “The figures point to a willingness among many young people to learn more about both language traditions and highlight the importance of creating opportunities for meaningful engagement with language, heritage and culture across all communities.”

text:
have heavily criticized Pete Buttigieg’s tenure as Transportation Secretary (Feb. 2021–Jan. 2025) for slow or inadequate responses to multiple crises, prioritization of DEI/equity/climate messaging over core safety and modernization, absences during key periods, and a pattern of deflecting blame. They portray a series of infrastructure, rail, aviation, and logistics failures as evidence of incompetence or misplaced priorities rather than just unavoidable events. Here is a factual list of major emergencies/incidents during his watch, paired with the primary right-leaning critiques of handling and context.Key Incidents and Critiques
East Palestine, Ohio, train derailment (Feb. 3, 2023): Norfolk Southern freight train carrying vinyl chloride and other hazardous materials derailed, leading to fire, controlled burn, evacuations, and ongoing environmental concerns. NTSB later called aspects preventable.
Right-leaning coverage emphasized that Buttigieg stayed silent for ~10 days (while discussing equity topics), did not visit for nearly three weeks, and initially downplayed it as one of ~1,000 annual derailments. Sen. Marco Rubio and others called for his resignation, citing a pattern of ignoring crises. Residents and local officials expressed feeling abandoned. He later acknowledged he “could have spoken sooner.” Critics noted he shifted blame to Trump-era regulatory https://t.co/0V8kB96aip

FAA NOTAM system outage / nationwide ground stop (Jan. 11, 2023): First full grounding of U.S. domestic flights since 9/11 (roughly 90 minutes). Caused by a damaged database file in the pilot notification system; thousands of delays/cancellations followed.
Conservative outlets highlighted long-standing warnings about outdated FAA systems and accused the department of focusing on renaming “Notice to Airmen” to the more “inclusive” “Notice to Air Missions” rather than technical upgrades. Later, when a similar 2026 nationwide ground stop occurred under the next administration, Buttigieg publicly questioned the lack of redundancies and offered to help travelers rebook—prompting accusations of hypocrisy from NY Post and others, who noted the prior outage happened on his watch and that modernization progress was https://t.co/7sJRU6JrQ3

Supply-chain / port congestion crisis (2021–2022): Major backlogs (especially Port of Los Angeles with 100+ ships at peak), product shortages, and inflation pressures.
Criticism centered on Buttigieg’s paternity leave during the height of the crisis (October 2021) and reports of limited high-level meetings on the issue for periods in late summer/fall 2021. He was accused of being absent while the problem affected https://t.co/K4IM3wbU8i
Southwest Airlines holiday meltdown (Dec. 2022): Nearly 17,000 cancellations, ~2 million passengers affected. DOT later imposed a large fine.
Framed as part of broader aviation reliability problems under his leadership, with questions about whether consumer protections or operational fixes were prioritized early enough.

I-95 collapse in Philadelphia (June 2023): Tanker truck fire under an overpass collapsed a major section (one fatality); temporary reopening in ~12 days.
Buttigieg visited and pledged support; some coverage was less critical of the response speed here compared to East Palestine, though it was still cited in broader lists of infrastructure failures.

Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse, Baltimore (March 2024): Ship strike caused collapse, deaths of construction workers, and major port/traffic disruption.
He was on-site quickly (contrasted positively by some with East Palestine), but the event was still grouped with other disasters as evidence of systemic issues during the administration.
Other recurring issues cited: Multiple additional train derailments (some involving hazardous materials), bridge collapses, air traffic controller shortages leading to flight cuts, Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack (May 2021, fuel shortages), and near-misses or operational problems in aviation. Near-averted rail strike (2022) also drew attention when he was reported vacationing in Portugal during negotiations.

text:
Beau Bayh promised in campaign commercials to "Get rid of corruption" in the state. What does he plan to do to deliver on his promise to Indiana voters who elected him? What does he plan to do with our election system in Indiana? What is his position on fraud, illegal aliens present in Indiana, crime in Indianapolis?

GROK says:

Beau Bayh (Democrat) was elected Indiana Secretary of State in November 2026 and is set to take office on January 1, 2027. He is the son of former Gov./Sen. Evan Bayh, a Harvard-educated attorney and former Marine Corps captain. His central campaign theme was cleaning up alleged corruption and waste in the outgoing Diego Morales (R) administration.
⁠Ballotpedia

Delivering on “Get rid of corruption”

Bayh’s top priority and repeated campaign promise focused on the Secretary of State’s office itself. He cited examples such as a roughly $92,000 luxury SUV, family members hired into high-paying roles, no-bid contracts linked to campaign donors, and questions about travel/spending.⁠
Indystar

His stated plans include:

Launching an independent/forensic audit of the office’s finances, contracts, travel, and hiring on day one (or immediately), with findings made public.
Referring any evidence of illegality to prosecutors/law enforcement.

Involving Republican Knox County Clerk David Shelton (described as a fraud-detection expert) to help oversee the audit for bipartisan credibility.

A personal pledge not to award Secretary of State contracts to his own campaign donors, plus competitively bidding contracts.

Additional ethics steps, such as barring campaign staff from contacting state employees about state business and prohibiting individual stock trading by      himself and top staff.⁠
Mirrorindy

These were framed as restoring trust after what he called insider dealing and waste under the prior Republican officeholder. Critics noted his own large out-of-state donations (including ties linked to his father’s network) and questioned whether the audit would be fully independent.⁠
Wndu

Plans for Indiana’s election system

Bayh’s main election-process proposals center on participation and competition rather than major new restrictions:

Ending  straight-ticket voting (Indiana is one of the few states that still has it). He argues this would force voters to consider individual candidates, increase competition, and raise turnout.

Supporting citizen-led ballot initiatives/referendums so voters can weigh in directly on issues (e.g., redistricting).

Preserving mail-in/absentee and early voting, with possible interest in extending Election Day hours for working families.

Supporting the state’s existing voter ID law and stating that Indiana elections are already “safe and secure,” crediting bipartisan county clerks.⁠
Wthitv

He has expressed skepticism about some federal proposals (such as certain proof-of-citizenship documentation requirements under ideas like the SAVE Act), calling some of them potentially burdensome or unnecessary given existing state systems, and has criticized unnecessary sharing of voter data with Washington without clear need.⁠
Insideindianabusiness

Position on fraud

Bayh has repeatedly said there should be “no illegal votes—period,” “one illegal vote is too many,” and that every instance of fraud should be prosecuted to the full extent of the law. He supports Indiana’s voter ID law as a safeguard. In debates he criticized the prior Republican administration for identifying potential noncitizen voting cases (including reports of noncitizens registered and some ballots cast) but not moving quickly to prosecution, while also calling some of his opponent’s framing of the issue “ridiculous” and saying current systems already prevent noncitizen voting (which is already illegal).
⁠Mirrorindy

Illegal aliens / noncitizens in Indiana

Bayh has not issued broad public positions on immigration enforcement, deportation, or the presence of illegal aliens outside the election context. The Secretary of State’s core duties are elections, business filings, and related administrative matters—not immigration enforcement (which involves federal agencies, the state Attorney General, and local law enforcement).

On the election-specific issue, his position is that noncitizen voting is illegal and should be prosecuted, existing voter ID helps prevent it, and elections are secure. He has pushed back against claims that stronger citizenship-verification steps are urgently needed beyond current law, describing some proposals as fear-mongering that could discourage legitimate participation.⁠
Cms.stateaffairs

Crime in Indianapolis
No specific positions or plans from Bayh on Indianapolis/Marion County crime rates, policing, or related issues appear in his campaign materials or coverage. Those matters fall outside the Secretary of State’s authority (they involve local government, the mayor, police, prosecutors, and the state Attorney General).

In short, Bayh’s concrete commitments center on auditing and reforming the Secretary of State’s office for alleged waste and self-dealing, plus process changes like ending straight-ticket voting and adding citizen initiatives, while affirming support for existing voter ID and prosecuting illegal votes. Broader topics like statewide immigration enforcement or Indianapolis crime were not central to his campaign messaging for this office.

How can Beau Bayh get rid of Straight ticket voting if voters in Indiana prefer it?

GROK says:

Beau Bayh cannot unilaterally eliminate straight-ticket voting.

It is established by Indiana state law, so only the General Assembly can repeal or change it. As Secretary of State (taking office January 1, 2027), Bayh has no authority to rewrite election statutes on his own.⁠
https://t.co/RQXrmb3XTX

He has described ending it as a legislative priority and noted that “there’s at least some Republicans in the Statehouse that agree with me.” He has framed it as a multi-year effort that would require working with the legislature, not something he could impose on day one. Recent attempts illustrate the challenge: Republican-authored bills such as HB 1133 (Rep. Cory Criswell) and HB 1218 (Rep. Edward Clere) to eliminate straight-ticket voting were introduced in 2026 but did not advance, while a bill expanding it (HB 1377) passed and became law. Prior efforts over the past decade have also failed.⁠
Indianacitizen

On whether Indiana voters prefer it

Bayh’s position is that the practice is poor policy regardless of short-term partisan effects. He argues it reduces competition, reinforces tribal “red team / blue team” voting, makes people feel outcomes are predetermined, and lowers incentives to participate or hold individual candidates accountable. He has said he supports ending it even though it could hurt Democrats in places like Marion County (where straight-ticket Democratic ballots far outnumbered Republican ones in 2026).⁠
Indianacapitalchronicle

Available polling does not show clear majority preference for keeping the system:

A October 2025 survey of 604 registered Indiana voters (North Star Opinion Research, for Independent Indiana) found 62% viewed straight-ticket voting as a “bad thing” versus 26% who called it a “good thing.” Even among Republicans, more viewed it negatively (49% bad / 36% good).

One Republican legislator (Criswell) reported that roughly 60% of respondents in his district survey supported eliminating it.

Usage is high where available—over 50% of voters in the largest counties in recent elections, and substantial shares in places like Marion County—but that reflects convenience when the option exists, not necessarily a preference for the policy itself. Indiana is one of only six states that still offer it (alongside Alabama, Kentucky, Michigan, Oklahoma, and South Carolina); most other states have eliminated it over the past few decades.
⁠https://t.co/d1VO8ZcW1Y

In short, Bayh’s path is advocacy and coalition-building in a Republican-controlled legislature, not executive fiat. Whether that succeeds depends on legislative votes, not on his preferences or any single poll.

My tenure as Bihar’s Tourism Minister during 2024–25 was a particularly memorable and enriching phase for me. It gave me the opportunity to travel, discover and appreciate our state’s remarkable diversity and the immense treasures it holds. The more I explored, the more I realised how much Bihar has to offer.

From the sacred birthplace of Maa Sita at Punaura Dham to the revered Vishnupad Temple in Gaya; from the spiritual destinations of Bodh Gaya and Rajgir to the ancient centres of learning at Nalanda and Vikramshila, Bihar has an extraordinary civilisational and spiritual legacy.

Beyond religious and heritage tourism, our state also offers immense possibilities in eco-tourism, water tourism and adventure tourism, with its beautiful hills, waterfalls, wildlife sanctuaries and the Valmiki Tiger Reserve.

Bihar is already working towards strengthening tourism infrastructure, improving connectivity and developing visitor facilities to ensure that tourists enjoy a comfortable, enriching and memorable experience.

I have always believed that Bihar’s tourism potential deserves much greater recognition. With our rich heritage, natural beauty and sustained efforts, we can bring these wonderful destinations to the attention of people across India and the world.

Bihar is not just a destination of history and pilgrimage; it is a state waiting to be explored in all its diversity.

Wishing you and your family a very happy and blessed Chhath Mahaparv, Shri Anand Mahindra ji!

text:
I came across this video of Rajgir in Bihar & was intrigued. 

I vaguely knew of Rajgir, but had never really thought of it as a tourist destination.

So I decided to read up a little more about it. 
It turned out to be a rewarding exploration.

Rajgir was the capital of Magadha over 2,500 years ago. The Buddha and Mahavira both spent time here. The city was once surrounded by a massive stone wall, almost 40 kilometres long, built without mortar.

Today, it has a spectacular glass skywalk, ropeways, forested hills and ancient monuments.

But my reading led me to think more broadly about Bihar itself.

Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment. Nalanda, one of the ancient world’s greatest centres of learning. Vaishali, associated with one of the earliest republican systems of government. And Pataliputra, capital of Ashoka’s Mauryan Empire.

An incredible concentration of history and heritage in one state

And yet, outside its important pilgrimage circuits, Bihar seems to receive relatively little attention as a tourist destination.

I can’t help feeling that Bihar is sitting on a tourism gold mine. 

All this reflection prompted by one video of Rajgir. A reminder of how much there still is to explore in our own country…

#SundayWanderer

text:
$UNI flipped short while its established daily regime was still rising strongly. Kong Score: 23, Noise tier.

This is a useful worked example of how Kong Cloud treats a counter-trend event when the surrounding structure has not yet turned with it.

The regime model identified a staircase of six steps across 158 bars, covering 34.14 ATR before the flip. That matters because Kong Cloud does not give every directional change the same structural meaning. In a strong trending regime, a counter-trend event begins with a structural factor of 0.35. The same event after a weak trend receives more credit because the prior direction has less structural persistence.

That 0.35 factor is the first restraint in today's reading. The system has detected a short state, but the broader frame still describes an established rise. The event is therefore evidence of tension inside the regime, not proof that the regime itself has changed.

Pattern evidence becomes especially important on this path. Kong's trending model assigns pattern a weight of 40, the largest component weight, because a recognized reversal formation can supply structural context that a cloud cross alone cannot. Edwards and Magee formalized the distinction between an ordinary interruption and a completed reversal structure. Bulkowski later measured formation behavior statistically. Kong uses that principle as a scoring hierarchy: the flip identifies a state change, while pattern evidence asks whether price structure supports a larger transition.

No reversal pattern was present at the frame's top for this prime. The pattern component therefore contributed 0.0. That absence is analytically meaningful because it leaves the counter-trend flip without the model's highest-weight source of confirmation.

Volume offered limited support. Activity measured 1.12 times the rolling baseline, inside Kong's normal 0.8x to 1.5x band, though its direction was increasing. The volume component contributed 12.0. This is participation, but not the expansion above 1.5x that moves into the confirmed band or above 2.0x that qualifies as strong.

The five-day macro view diverged and contributed 0.6. Regime contributed 5.0, while structural context added 5.25. Together with volume, those inputs produced the final score of 23.

The indicator construction matters here too. Wilder's smoothing family reduces sensitivity to isolated price movement, while confirmation logic is designed to prevent every cross from becoming a new state. Murphy's treatment of confirmation offers the broader principle: evidence becomes more informative when independent dimensions agree. Today's dimensions do not agree. Direction flipped short, the regime remained strongly established in the other direction, macro diverged, and no reversal formation appeared.

The next useful information is structural. Does the short state persist long enough to alter the staircase, or does the existing regime absorb the interruption? Until price structure answers that question, the low score is doing exactly what the methodology intends: recording the flip while preserving uncertainty about its significance.

text:
Erwin Rommel, born in Germany in 1891, was a controversial German field marshal in World War II, known as the "Desert Fox".

Rommel joined the army in his early years and fought on the front lines in World War I, earning medals for his bravery. He remained in the military after the war and wrote Infantry Attacks. His unique tactical ideas won him Hitler’s favour. During the Battle of France in 1940, he commanded the 7th Panzer Division, striking rapidly with lightning advances. His division became famous as the "Ghost Division", and Rommel rose to prominence overnight.

In 1941, Rommel was sent to North Africa to take charge of the crumbling German‑Italian forces. Outnumbered and poorly supplied, he repeatedly defeated the British army with flexible and mobile tactics and advanced all the way to Tobruk, reaching the height of his fame. Yet his supply lines eventually collapsed. Defeated by Montgomery at El Alamein, he had to lead his troops in a gradual withdrawal from North Africa. Back in Europe, he oversaw the construction of the Atlantic Wall to defend against an Allied landing. After the Normandy landings, the German lines quickly crumbled. Rommel was seriously wounded when his car was strafed by enemy aircraft.

In his later years, Rommel grew increasingly disillusioned with the course of the war and Hitler. He was implicated in the 20 July plot to assassinate Hitler. Though he had not taken part in the assassination itself, Hitler offered him two choices: stand public trial and bring ruin to his family, or take his own life honourably in return for guaranteed benefits for his loved ones. On 14 October 1944, Rommel died by poison. His death was officially announced as a result of his battle injuries.

Rommel was a brilliant tactician. He liked to command from the front, often fought against greater odds, and cared for his soldiers. Even his opponents admired his military skill. Nevertheless, he served as an instrument of Nazi aggression. The so‑called "Rommel myth" passed down to later generations contains much propaganda and glorification. He refused orders to carry out massacres and racial purges, yet became entangled in the plot against Hitler. This contradictory image has made him one of the most discussed figures of the Second World War.

text:
TIME TO LOOK AHEAD: With Lincoln Riley’s future at #USC facing growing uncertainty, the Trojans could emerge as one of the biggest players in the 2027 college football coaching carousel.

Should USC decide to move in a different direction, several intriguing names could enter the conversation.

Here are my top-five coaching candidates, ranked by overall fit, coaching résumé, recruiting potential, and realistic availability:

• KALEN DEBOER — ALABAMA (HC)
Led Washington to the national championship game and was previously hired by USC athletic director Jen Cohen. The connection is intriguing, but would DeBoer consider leaving Alabama for Los Angeles?

• KALANI SITAKE — BYU (HC)
A defensive-minded culture builder who emphasizes physicality and discipline. Sitake would represent a significant philosophical shift from Riley, although his commitment to BYU could make him difficult to land.

• RHETT LASHLEE — SMU (HC)
An accomplished offensive mind with CFP experience. His offensive philosophy fits USC’s identity, but convincing him to leave SMU could prove challenging.

• SPENCER DANIELSON — BOISE STATE (HC)
A defensive-minded coach with California ties and CFP experience. Danielson offers an intriguing combination of physical football, strong leadership, and a culture-first approach.

• GLENN SCHUMANN — GEORGIA (DC)
An elite defensive coordinator with experience under Kirby Smart and Nick Saban. Schumann could transform USC’s defensive identity and strengthen recruiting, although he lacks head-coaching experience.

If USC ultimately parts ways with Lincoln Riley, its next coaching hire could define the program’s future for years to come. The opportunity to restore one of college football’s most storied programs to national prominence would come with enormous expectations.

📸: Ken Lambert / The Seattle Times
